passage: Last Holi, a gang of us from Class 5 ran through the colony with water balloons. I'm Manoj, and on my own I'm quite quiet. But in that noisy crowd, all of us purple and green, it felt as if nobody could tell who was who. When we saw Uma hiding behind her gate because she hates colour, someone started chanting 'Scaredy Uma!' and I chanted too, louder than anyone. I even threw a balloon at the gate. Alone, I would never have done that. Uma is my neighbour; she lends me comics. She ran inside crying. Afterwards, washing off the colour, I felt sick. In the crowd it hadn't felt like me doing it. But it was. The next day I went and said sorry, and gave her my best comic.

qa.q: Why was Uma hiding behind her gate?
qa.a: Because she hates colour.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel washing off the colour afterwards?
qa.a: Manoj felt sick and ashamed, knowing he had joined in teasing he would never do alone.

qa.q: What could Manoj do next time a crowd starts chanting?
qa.a: He could remember that it's still him in the crowd, stay quiet or step out, and stand with the person being teased.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt hearing her neighbour chant with the crowd?
qa.a: Uma likely felt hurt and betrayed, since Manoj was a friend who borrowed her comics.

grounding: A boy looks back on joining a Holi crowd's teasing he would never do alone, feeling hidden in the group.

passage:
Class 6 note, winter picnic bus.
On the way back from the zoo, the back of the bus started chanting a rhyme about Vijay's thick glasses. It began with two boys and spread fast. I noticed Leela, who is usually gentle and had read quietly all the way there, singing loudest and banging the seat. When I walked down, it stopped. Leela went red and looked at the floor. She told me later, 'Everyone was doing it. It didn't feel like me.' Vijay sat with his face to the window. I sat next to him for the rest of the ride. At school I spoke to the back rows together, then to Leela alone; she asked to apologise to Vijay herself. I phoned Vijay's mother this evening and will check in with him tomorrow.

qa.q: What was the rhyme about?
qa.a: Vijay's thick glasses.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the teacher walked down the aisle?
qa.a: Leela felt embarrassed and ashamed, going red and looking at the floor.

qa.a: It stopped the chant, stayed with Vijay, spoke to the group and then to Leela privately, and let Leela make her own apology.

qa.q: What was the ride like for Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay felt hurt and humiliated, sitting with his face to the window while most of the bus sang about him.

passage:
Diwali night.
Dear diary, I did something bad. On the terrace, all the colony kids were bursting crackers and being loud, and somebody started laughing at Keerthana's frock because it was last year's. Then everybody laughed, and somehow I was laughing too, and I even said 'hand-me-down queen'. It was dark and smoky and nobody could see who said what, and it felt like the noise said it, not me. Keerthana went downstairs. Then I saw her mother's face at the door. My stomach dropped. Keerthana helped me with fractions all summer! Amma asked why I was quiet, and I told her. She didn't shout. She said, 'Your name goes with you, even in the dark.' Tomorrow I'll go and say sorry, and take her some of our kaju katli.
Leela

qa.q: Why were the kids laughing at Keerthana's frock?
qa.a: Because it was last year's.

qa.q: What did Leela feel on seeing Keerthana's mother at the door?
qa.a: Leela felt a sinking guilt, stomach dropping, realising the teasing had hurt someone who had been kind.

qa.q: What does Amma's line 'Your name goes with you, even in the dark' teach?
qa.a: That being part of a noisy crowd doesn't remove responsibility; Leela still chose the words.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt going downstairs?
qa.a: Keerthana probably felt humiliated and hurt, mocked by a crowd that included someone she had helped.

grounding: A child's Diwali diary shows joining crowd teasing on a dark terrace and feeling it wasn't really them.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: It was 1 am, three days before the board exams, and Farida should have been asleep. Instead she was scrolling the school's anonymous confessions page, where someone had posted an unflattering photo of Sachin tripping at sports day. Two hundred comments already. Everyone was piling on. Farida's thumb hovered. Sachin had once corrected her in front of the class, and she had never forgiven him. She typed something mean about his walk and hit send. No name, just a cartoon avatar. For a second it felt like nothing, one more voice. Then she read it back, and it looked like something a stranger had written. But it was hers. She deleted it at 1:04 and lay awake. In the morning she messaged Sachin under her real name: 'I said something cruel on the page last night. I'm sorry. I've reported the post.'

qa.q: How many comments did the post already have?
qa.a: Two hundred comments.

passage: The stadium in Kolkata was packed for the inter-school final, and Siddharth's section was a sea of blue. When the rival captain, a tall boy called Mridul, dropped a catch, the whole stand started chanting an ugly word about his skin. Siddharth, who would never say that to anyone's face, found himself shouting it too, fists in the air, his voice lost among two thousand others. It felt like the crowd was shouting, not him. Then Mridul turned, and for a second Siddharth saw his face clearly: not a villain, just a boy his age, blinking hard. Siddharth's throat closed. He stopped chanting. The boy beside him nudged him. 'Come on!' Siddharth shook his head and sat down. That evening he wrote to the school's sports teacher about the chant.

passage:
'Did you see the class group last night?' Jyoti asked, dropping her bag beside Reena's.
'The dance video? Everyone was laughing.'
'You too. You sent twenty laughing faces and "cringe queen".'
Reena shrugged. 'Everyone was. It's just a group chat.'
'Meenal left the group at midnight. She's absent today.'
Reena's smile faded. 'I didn't even say anything that bad.'
'Forty people each said something small. That's forty things landing on one person.'
'It didn't feel like me. It was all the others.'
'Your name is on it, Reena. It's the same you in there.'
Reena stared at her phone. 'Should I message her?'
'Yes. Delete your comments. And we tell Ma'am at lunch.'
At lunch the class teacher listened, phoned Meenal's mother that afternoon and had the group closed.

passage: It started with one screenshot. By 9 pm last April, my phone had a hundred and forty messages from numbers I didn't know, all about a rumour that I had cheated in the science exam. I'm Jasleen, and I've never been so frightened of a buzzing sound. There was no one person to explain to; every time I replied to one, ten more came. It was like drowning in a crowd without faces. I put the phone in a drawer and sat on the bathroom floor. My cousin Gurpreet found me and didn't ask questions. She took the phone, sat with me and called my mother in from the kitchen. Mummy read ten messages, took screenshots, blocked the numbers and phoned my class teacher that same night. The next morning the principal spoke to the class. The messages stopped. I still flinch at notifications sometimes.

qa.q: How many messages had Jasleen received by 9 pm?
qa.a: A hundred and forty messages from unknown numbers.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel as the messages kept coming?
qa.a: Jasleen felt frightened and overwhelmed, like drowning in a crowd without faces.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped?
qa.a: She saved screenshots, blocked the numbers and phoned the class teacher that same night, so adults could act quickly.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet help?
qa.a: Gurpreet stayed calm, didn't ask questions, sat with Jasleen and brought Mummy in right away.

grounding: A teenager recalls being mobbed by anonymous messages with no one to reason with, and the same-night adult response.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Tuesday, 3:40 pm.
Varun brought Mahima to my office after lunch. About fifteen senior students had surrounded her near the canteen, shouting about a post they believed she had written about their teacher. Mahima said she tried to explain, but each time she spoke to one, others shouted over her. 'There was no one to talk to. Just noise.' She was shaking and hadn't eaten. I stayed with her, got her water and food, and told her plainly that this was not her fault. With her agreement I informed the vice-principal, who spoke to the senior group before dismissal, and I phoned her mother, who collected her at 4. Varun stayed with her until then. Plan: the vice-principal meets the seniors' parents tomorrow; I will see Mahima first thing in the morning.

qa.q: How many seniors surrounded Mahima?
qa.a: About fifteen senior students.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when every attempt to explain was shouted over?
qa.a: Mahima felt overwhelmed and frightened, shaking because there was no single person to reason with.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's response strong?
qa.a: Staying with Mahima, telling her it wasn't her fault, and informing the vice-principal and her mother the same afternoon.

qa.q: What did Varun do for Mahima?
qa.a: Varun brought her to the counsellor and stayed with her until her mother came, so she wasn't alone.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a student overwhelmed by a hostile crowd of seniors and the same-day protective response.

passage:
Saturday night.
Diary, today was the worst. I posted my first comic on the art site, and by lunch it had three hundred comments. Not nice ones. Someone shared it to a big meme page, and strangers were calling my drawing trash, telling me to quit, pasting my face into jokes. I kept refreshing, trying to answer, but for every one I answered, twenty more came. There's nobody to argue with in a crowd like that. I cried so hard I got hiccups. My brother Naveen saw my face at dinner and made me show him. He didn't laugh. He went straight to Papa. Papa helped me set the post to private, report the page and block everyone, and he said, 'None of these people know you. We do.' He sat with me till I fell asleep. Tomorrow we tell my art teacher too.
Hansa

qa.q: How many comments did the comic have by lunch?
qa.a: Three hundred comments.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel as the comments kept coming?
qa.a: Hansa felt overwhelmed and crushed, crying till hiccups came, with no one to reason with in the crowd.

qa.q: What did Papa's response get right?
qa.a: He acted that same evening: making the post private, reporting the page, blocking, reassuring Hansa and staying close until sleep.

qa.q: How did Naveen react when he saw Hansa's face?
qa.a: Naveen was worried and serious, didn't laugh, and went straight to Papa.

grounding: A teenager's diary records being mobbed online by strangers with no one to reason with, and the family's same-evening response.

subtype: Noticing the slide in a group [Observer]
passage: I'm Santosh, and I was at the Holi party on the college ground last March. For the first hour it was perfect: music, colour, everyone dancing. Then someone brought a crate of eggs and a bucket of muddy water, and the mood tipped. People started targeting the first-years who hadn't wanted to play, dragging them in, laughing. My friend Alka had just smeared a boy's face with mud and was reaching for more. I could see that nobody there would do that on an ordinary Tuesday. It was the crowd, the noise, the colour on every face. I took Alka by the arm. 'Look at him.' The first-year was crying. She stopped and dropped the mud. We took him to the tap and then to the hostel warden, who shut the gate on the egg crate. I still don't know what Alka was thinking in that moment.

qa.q: What did someone bring that changed the mood?
qa.a: A crate of eggs and a bucket of muddy water.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel as the mood tipped?
qa.a: Santosh felt uneasy and alarmed, seeing people act in ways they never would on an ordinary day.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that helped?
qa.a: Santosh noticed early, made Alka look at the first-year, helped him and told the warden, who stopped the eggs.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt when she saw the crying first-year?
qa.a: Alka probably felt a jolt of shame, stopping and dropping the mud when she saw him clearly.

passage:
Monday: Parul joined the student march for fair hostel fees, placard in hand. It was peaceful, with songs, and she felt a little proud.
Wednesday: the second march was bigger, and the mood had changed. Someone started throwing stones at the admin block's windows. Parul saw Eshaan, a quiet boy from her physics class who apologised when he bumped into chairs, pick up a stone. His face looked like someone else's. The crowd roared. Parul's stomach knotted. She grabbed Eshaan's sleeve. 'This isn't what we came for. Walk with me.' He hesitated, then dropped the stone, and they stepped out to the pavement.
The next Monday: at the organising meeting, Parul proposed marshals with armbands and a rule to leave if anyone turned violent. Eshaan volunteered first. 'I don't know what happened to me on Wednesday,' he said quietly.

qa.q: What was the march for?

qa.q: What did Parul feel when she saw Eshaan pick up a stone?
qa.a: Parul felt alarmed, her stomach knotting at the change in a gentle classmate and the crowd's roar.

qa.a: It helps the group notice the slide early and gives people a clear way to leave or calm others before things turn reckless.

qa.a: Eshaan seems unsettled and regretful, unsure what happened to him, and volunteers as a marshal.

subtype: Noticing the slide in a group [Observer]
passage: Avni, you're off to the victory celebration tonight, so let me tell you about a night when I was twenty. Our college team won the state final, and half of Aligarh poured into the streets. Drums, sweets, dancing on car roofs. Beautiful. Then around midnight it changed. A boy set fire to a rival college's banner; others started kicking shop shutters. I saw my friend Rashid, who cried at sad films, climbing a lamp post to rip down a sign. In a crowd like that you stop being a person and become part of a noise. I felt the pull too. Then I thought of my mother's face if she saw me. So I stood under Rashid's lamp post and said, 'Come down, let's get chai.' He looked at me like someone waking up. We walked away. Irfan Chacha's rule, beta: notice the moment the mood turns, and leave early.

qa.q: What did the boy set fire to?
qa.a: A rival college's banner.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel as the mood changed?
qa.a: Irfan felt uneasy and felt the crowd's pull too, until thinking of his mother's face steadied him.

qa.q: Irfan chose to stand under the lamp post and invite Rashid for chai. Why was that a good turning point?
qa.a: It calmly pulled Rashid out of the crowd's pull with something ordinary, so both left before doing something they'd regret.

qa.q: How might Rashid have felt when Irfan called him down?
qa.a: Rashid probably felt like waking up, suddenly aware of what he was doing and relieved to walk away.

passage: I'm Aadhya, and I work on the same floor as Akash. Last month a colleague from another team made an embarrassing mistake in a client email, and someone forwarded it to the big office chat with a mocking caption. Within minutes there were fifty replies: memes, jokes, people who had never met her. I sent a laughing face myself. Akash didn't. I watched him type, delete, type again. Then he posted, in his own words: 'We've all sent a bad email. She's a person on the fourth floor, not a meme. I'm out of this thread.' And he left the chat. A few people grumbled that he was preachy. But the jokes slowed. Later I saw him walk up to her desk with a coffee. I don't know what was in his head. I deleted my laughing face that evening.

qa.q: How many replies were there within minutes?
qa.a: Fifty replies.

qa.q: What might Akash have been feeling as he typed and deleted?
qa.a: Akash was probably uneasy and torn, weighing the crowd's mood against his own conscience before choosing his words.

qa.q: What makes Akash's reply a good model?
qa.a: He spoke in his own name, reminded everyone she was a real person, and stepped away from the pile-on.

qa.q: How did watching Akash affect Aadhya?
qa.a: Aadhya felt uncomfortable about the laughing face and deleted it that evening.

subtype: Keeping the self in the crowd [Response]
passage:
Friday, a week before Suraj's wedding: Tejas told himself, as he often did, 'My name goes with me.' He had started saying it after a college night he still regretted.
The wedding night: the baraat danced through the Jaipur lane, drums thundering, forty cousins in pink turbans. Someone knocked over a fruit seller's cart and the crowd laughed and kept dancing, stepping on oranges. Suraj's cousins started throwing the fruit at each other. The old seller stood frozen. Tejas felt the pull to keep dancing, one pink turban among forty. He stopped. He stepped out of the procession, knelt and began picking up oranges. Suraj saw and came over. They paid the seller for the damage, apologised and rejoined the baraat.
Two days later: the seller turned up at the reception with a basket of fresh oranges as a gift. Suraj hugged Tejas. 'You saved my wedding's name.'

qa.q: How many cousins were in pink turbans?
qa.a: Forty cousins.

qa.q: What did Tejas feel as the crowd laughed at the cart?
qa.a: Tejas felt the pull to keep dancing along, but also uneasy, remembering that his name went with him.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that others could copy?
qa.a: He stepped out of the crowd, helped the seller and brought the groom along to repair the harm.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller have felt when Tejas knelt to help?

subtype: Keeping the self in the crowd [Response]
passage: Hemant, you're starting at the new company tomorrow, with all its group chats and team rituals, so listen to an old woman. When I was twenty-four, a new teacher at a big school in Pune, the staff had a welcome tradition for newcomers: everyone crowded into the staff room and made the new person sing, dance and answer silly personal questions. It seemed like fun. Then one year the newcomer was a shy young man with a stammer. The crowd laughed and pushed him to speak faster. I laughed too, at first. Then I heard myself, and I thought: Minakshi, would you do this alone? I stood up and said, 'That's enough. Let him sit.' It went quiet. Some colleagues didn't speak to me for a week. But that young man became my closest friend on the staff, and together we ended the tradition the next year.

qa.q: What did the staff make newcomers do?
qa.a: Sing, dance and answer silly personal questions.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel when she heard herself laughing?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and ashamed, realising she was doing something she would never do alone.

qa.q: Minakshi stood up and said 'That's enough. Let him sit.' Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It broke the crowd's spell by speaking in her own name, protecting the young man and later ending the tradition.

qa.q: How might the young man with the stammer have felt when Minakshi spoke up?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and grateful to be rescued from the laughing crowd.

grounding: An elder recalls stepping out of a staff-room crowd's teasing in her own name when it began to hurt someone.

passage: Two weeks after Avni became Class 9B's monitor, the room felt different. She stood at the front during free period, writing names on the board for anyone who whispered. She sent Keerthana to the corridor for asking to borrow a pen. She moved her own seat to the window, which had always gone by turn. When Keerthana said, 'You weren't like this before,' Avni didn't even look up from the register. 'Rules are rules.' But she let her own friend leave early for dance practice. That evening she felt a small glow reading the names on her list, twelve of them. It didn't occur to her that nobody had laughed near her all week.

passage:
Dear Arnab,
Captaincy is AMAZING. You were right to recommend me. I've already changed everything on the basketball team. Practice is now at 6 am, because I'm fastest in the mornings. I've moved Riddhi to the bench; she argues too much. When Neelima said the 6 am slot is hard for players who take the bus from far away, I told her real players adjust. Coach Sharma says I'm very decisive. The juniors run when I blow the whistle. It's a nice feeling, people doing what you say. Some of them are sulking, but that's their problem. Honestly, I don't remember you having this much trouble with the team. Maybe they just like me less? Anyway, come and watch Saturday's match. We'll win.
Tanuja

passage: You asked about being head girl. Honestly? I'm Minakshi, seventeen, and it changed me faster than I'd like to admit. In the first month I loved it: teachers calling me by name, juniors going quiet when I walked in. I started telling people how to line up, what to wear for assemblies, even how to speak to me. When the Class 8 kids complained about losing their lunch-break football for my discipline drive, I told them to stop whining. I didn't notice I'd stopped asking anyone anything. Then my best friend Sangeeta said, in the canteen, 'You talk to us like we're files now.' That stung. I went home and read back my messages from that month. She was right. Every message was an order.

qa.q: What did the Class 8 kids lose because of the discipline drive?
qa.a: Their lunch-break football.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when Sangeeta said 'You talk to us like we're files now'?

qa.a: Start asking juniors for their views and give back the football break, so the role serves people rather than control.

In the lab meeting she took credit for their data cleaning without thinking. If anyone had asked, she would have said she was still the friendly Trisha from the canteen. Pradeep, eating alone by the sink window, no longer thought so.

qa.a: To wash glassware.

qa.q: What does Trisha feel about herself during these months?
qa.a: Trisha feels unchanged and comfortable, believing she is still the friendly Trisha from the canteen.

qa.q: What small changes could bring back Trisha's care for the helpers?
qa.a: Letting Pradeep attend talks, sharing credit for their work and keeping the same hours as the helpers.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel about the new Trisha?
qa.a: Pradeep feels hurt and resentful, eating alone and no longer seeing her as friendly.

grounding: A young intern given a little authority grows less attentive to juniors and bends rules for herself without noticing.

passage: By month-end at the Mumbai firm, Santosh had learned to read Afreen Ma'am's moods from the corridor: fast heels meant trouble, silence meant worse. Today it was both, and the tax filing was due at six. When she asked if his draft was ready, he said, 'Almost, Ma'am,' though he thought her approach to one clause was wrong. He had tried disagreeing once in March; she had cut him off in front of the whole team, and he still remembered the heat in his face. So now he said only what pleased her. At 5:40 she found the error he had seen hours ago. 'Why didn't anyone flag this?' Santosh looked at his shoes. He had flagged it. In his head. He went home feeling a little smaller, as he had every month since March.

qa.q: When was the tax filing due?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel going home?
qa.a: Santosh felt small and discouraged, having hidden a concern he knew was right.

qa.q: What could Santosh try next time?
qa.a: Raise the concern early in writing, politely and with reasons, so it is on record without a face-to-face clash.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel on finding the error at 5:40?
qa.a: Afreen likely felt frustrated and alarmed, not realising her team was too afraid to flag problems.

grounding: Under a deadline a junior employee reads a powerful boss's moods, hides his view and feels smaller for it.

passage: At the Bengaluru agency everyone knew the rule: when Saurabh Sir walked in, you checked his face first. Yusuf, eight months into his first job, had learned it faster than most. If Saurabh was smiling, you could suggest an idea. If he was frowning, you nodded at whatever he said. Yusuf had a campaign idea he believed in, for the tea client, but he had never pitched it; the one time he spoke up in a meeting, Saurabh had said, 'Did I ask you?' Now Yusuf laughed at Saurabh's jokes a beat too early and praised slides he found weak. At home his flatmate asked what he had done at work. 'Agreed with people,' Yusuf said, and felt oddly tired, like a lamp turned down.

qa.q: What did Saurabh say when Yusuf spoke up in a meeting?
qa.a: 'Did I ask you?'

qa.q: How does Yusuf feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Yusuf feels oddly tired and diminished, like a lamp turned down.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do to share the campaign idea safely?
qa.a: He could write it up and send it when things are calm, or ask a supportive senior to review it first.

qa.q: What might Saurabh not realise about his team?
qa.a: Saurabh may not realise his moods make people hide ideas and agree falsely, so he loses good work.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful boss's moods, hides his ideas and feels diminished.

passage:
'You didn't say anything in the meeting,' Ujjwal whispered at the pantry. 'You told me yesterday the vendor plan was a disaster.'
'It is.' Indu stirred her tea. 'But did you see his face? The vein thing.'
'So?'
'So when the vein thing happens, I agree.'
'Since when are you like this? At college you argued with professors for fun.'
Indu was quiet. 'Since the review. He said I was not a team player because I questioned his numbers. In front of everyone.'
'So now you just smile?'
'I smile. I say "good point, Sir". I check his mood before I send any email.' She laughed, but it came out thin. 'I feel like I've shrunk a size.'
Ujjwal leaned on the counter. 'Want to send the vendor concerns together? Two names. Harder to brush off.'
Indu looked at him for a long moment. 'Maybe.'

qa.q: What did the boss call Indu at the review?
qa.a: Not a team player.

qa.q: How does Indu feel about how she has changed?
qa.a: Indu feels diminished and a little sad, as if shrunk a size, watching the boss's moods and hiding her views.

qa.q: Why might Ujjwal's idea of sending the concerns together help?
qa.a: Two names are harder to brush off and give Indu support, so she can raise a real problem without facing him alone.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see the change in Indu?
qa.a: Ujjwal is surprised and concerned, remembering how she argued with professors for fun at college.

grounding: A young employee under a powerful boss has become watchful and quiet, and a colleague offers to speak up together.

passage: Rekha, you're worried because your friend got promoted and has stopped listening. Let me tell you about Joginder. We joined the textile mill in Ludhiana together at twenty-four and shared a tiffin for three years. Then he became shift manager. Within months he interrupted everyone, walked past our old lunch spot and expected his tea brought to his desk. The others gossiped about him in the dyeing shed. I nearly joined in. Instead, one evening, I waited for him at the gate and said, 'Joginder, you've stopped letting people finish their sentences. Even me.' He was angry at first. Then he admitted the owners were pressing him hard every day and he felt he had to look strong. We walked home together like old times. The next week he came back to the lunch spot. Vaibhav's advice, beta: say it to his face, kindly, and remember the pressure on him too.

qa.q: How long did Vaibhav and Joginder share a tiffin?
qa.a: For three years.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav feel watching Joginder change?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt hurt and was tempted to gossip, missing his old friend.

qa.q: Vaibhav chose to speak to Joginder at the gate instead of gossiping. Why was that the right turning point?
qa.a: It named the change honestly and kindly, gave Joginder a chance to explain the pressure, and brought him back to his old friends.

qa.q: How did Joginder feel when Vaibhav spoke to him?
qa.a: Joginder was angry at first, then honest, admitting the owners' pressure made him feel he had to look strong.

grounding: An elder recalls watching a friend change after promotion and gently naming it to his face while allowing for the pressure.

passage: Christmas week at the Aizawl hotel was chaos: full bookings, a broken boiler, and a new front-office manager, Tenzin, who until October had been Lalremsiami's desk partner and closest friend at work. Siami had watched him change in eight weeks. He interrupted guests mid-sentence, snapped at the housekeeping staff and expected everyone to cover his breaks while never covering theirs. The others whispered in the laundry room. On the 24th, when he cut off a junior in front of a guest, Siami felt her face burn. She waited until the boiler mechanic had gone and caught Tenzin alone by the back stairs. 'You've stopped listening, Tenzin. To all of us. I miss my friend.' He opened his mouth to argue, then slumped against the wall. 'The owners call me every hour. I feel like if I'm soft, I'm finished.' Siami nodded. 'Then be tired with us. Not at us.'

qa.q: What broke during Christmas week?
qa.a: The boiler.

qa.q: What did Siami feel when Tenzin cut off the junior?
qa.a: Siami felt embarrassed and upset, her face burning at her friend's rudeness.

qa.q: What made Siami's approach better than the whispering in the laundry room?
qa.a: She spoke to Tenzin directly and privately, named the change kindly and listened to the pressure behind it.

qa.q: Why had Tenzin been acting this way, according to him?
qa.a: Tenzin felt pressured by the owners' hourly calls and afraid that being soft would finish him.

grounding: In a busy festive week a young woman watches her friend change as a new manager and names it gently instead of gossiping.

passage: Anjali and Siddharth had been hired the same month at the Mumbai startup, and for two years they did everything together: late-night bug fixes, vada pav runs, complaining about bad managers. In June, Siddharth became team lead. By September, Anjali barely recognised him. He talked over people at stand-ups, took the corner cabin and replied to messages with single letters. When a junior asked him a question, he answered while typing. The team started a private chat to complain. Anjali muted it. On Friday she suggested their old vada pav walk, and on the way she said, 'Can I tell you something as your friend? You've stopped letting people finish. Me too.' He stopped walking. 'Seriously?' 'Seriously. I know the founders are on you all day.' He was quiet for a whole lane. 'Tell me when I do it again. Please.'

qa.q: What did Siddharth take after becoming team lead?
qa.a: The corner cabin.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel by September?
qa.a: Anjali felt saddened and uneasy, barely recognising the friend she had worked beside for two years.

qa.q: Why was muting the complaint chat and talking to Siddharth wise?
qa.a: It avoided gossip and gave him honest, private feedback from a friend, with understanding of the pressure he was under.

qa.q: How did Siddharth react to Anjali's words?
qa.a: Siddharth was surprised, then quiet and receptive, asking her to tell him when he did it again.

grounding: A young woman sees a friend change after becoming a manager and names it kindly in private rather than joining gossip.

passage: When Deepak was elected head of the farmers' cooperative in Sangola at twenty-five, the oldest member, Madhav Kaka, warned him: 'The chair changes people. Watch yourself.' Deepak took it seriously. He kept eating lunch at the same tea stall with the farmers, not in the new office. He put a box outside the office door for anonymous complaints and read every slip on Sunday. Before deciding the new water-sharing schedule, he walked the fields at the tail end of the canal, asking the smallest farmers what the change would cost them. When the plan worked, he stood back at the meeting and said, 'Madhav Kaka and the tail-end farmers designed this.' Madhav Kaka, who had argued with him at every meeting, grinned. 'Still the same boy. Good.'

qa.q: Where did Deepak keep eating lunch?
qa.a: At the same tea stall with the farmers.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt hearing Madhav Kaka's warning?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt respect mixed with caution, taking the warning seriously enough to build habits against it.

qa.q: Which habits kept Deepak humble?
qa.a: Eating with the farmers, reading anonymous complaints, asking the smallest farmers about costs and sharing credit publicly.

qa.q: How does Madhav Kaka see Deepak after the meeting?
qa.a: Madhav Kaka is pleased and proud, seeing that the chair hasn't changed Deepak.

grounding: A young cooperative head in a village guards against power's drift by staying close, inviting critics and sharing credit.

passage: When Siddiq became the youngest manager at the Warsaw logistics office, he wrote three rules on a sticky note inside his desk drawer: Ask who pays. Keep a critic. Give the credit away. His critic was Marek, a warehouse supervisor twenty years older who had openly doubted he could do the job. Siddiq invited him to every planning meeting. 'Tell me when I'm wrong,' he said. Marek did, often. When Siddiq wanted to move the night shift to cut costs, Marek said the older drivers couldn't sleep in the day. Siddiq went to the warehouse at 3 am and asked the drivers himself. He changed the plan. At the quarterly meeting, when the new routes saved money, he put Marek's name on the first slide. Marek grunted. 'You're less annoying than I expected.'

qa.q: What three rules did Siddiq write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Ask who pays. Keep a critic. Give the credit away.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when he invited his doubter to every meeting?
qa.a: Siddiq felt humble and curious, wanting honest criticism to guard against his own blind spots.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do before changing the night shift?
qa.a: He went to the warehouse at 3 am, asked the drivers himself, and then changed the plan.

qa.q: How does Marek's view of Siddiq change?
qa.a: Marek goes from openly doubting Siddiq to grudging respect, saying he's less annoying than expected.

grounding: A young manager abroad keeps a critic close, asks what decisions cost those below him and shares credit.
